To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
opioid analgesia can be mediated through two subpopulations of receptors, and that mu1 receptors mediate analgesia primarily through a supraspinal pathway.

the analgesia of a series of opioid compounds is mediated by two different populations of opioid binding sites in the mouse, and that these sites are located in the spinal cord and supraspinally, respectively.

the selective blockade of high affinity opioid receptors in vivo by naloxazones produces a differential shift of the analgesic ED(50) values for a series of opioid analgesics, suggesting a different subpopulation is involved in analgesia than in normal controls.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the pharmacological and anatomical basis for the analgesic action of opioid drugs.
the role of opioid receptors in analgesia.
the role of subtypes of opioid receptors in analgesia and tolerance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
naloxazone selectively blocked the analgesic action of opiates and opioids in the mouse through a supraspinal action of mu1 receptors.
the mu1 opioid receptors mediate analgesia primarily through a supraspinal mechanism, and that delta receptors may mediate some analgesia in mice.
the mu1 opioid analgesia is primarily supraspinals and is mediated through a subpopulation of opioid binding sites different from that mediating mu1 analgesic effects in normal animals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mu1 analagesia is supraspinal and delta-mediated, and mu2 analgesia is spinal and mu-mediated.
the mu1 opioid binding site mediates supraspinal analgesia in a manner that is dependent on the specific opioid agonist involved.
mu1 opioid receptors in the mouse mediate supraspinal analgesia and that delta opioid receptors are primarily involved in the spinal analgesic effects of opioids and opioid peptides.
The main takeaway from our work is that
opioid analgesics are mediated by multiple opioid receptor subtypes and that the opioid receptor subtypes that mediate analgesia are different in different species.
the mu1 opioid receptor is not the primary mediator of opioid analgesia.
the opioid analgesia is mediated by multiple subtypes of opioid receptors.
